claim: PAN-1 is a leucine-rich-repeat domain transmembrane protein required for synaptic rewiring in C. elegans.
source: We have identified a leucine-rich-repeat domain transmembrane protein PAN-1 as a factor required for synaptic rewiring in C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: PAN-1 localizes on cell membrane.
source: PAN-1 localizes on cell membrane and binds with MYRF, a membrane-bound transcription factor indispensable for promoting synaptic rewiring.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations in the results section.

claim: MYRF is a membrane-bound transcription factor indispensable for promoting synaptic rewiring.
source: PAN-1 localizes on cell membrane and binds with MYRF, a membrane-bound transcription factor indispensable for promoting synaptic rewiring.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by previous work cited in the introduction.

claim: Full-length MYRF undergoes self-cleavage on ER membrane and releases its transcriptional N-terminal fragment in cultured cells.
source: Full-length MYRF was known to undergo self-cleavage on ER membrane and release its transcriptional N-terminal fragment in cultured cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from prior research.

claim: MYRF trafficking to cell membrane before cleavage is pivotal for C. elegans development.
source: We surprisingly find that MYRF trafficking to cell membrane before cleavage is pivotal for C. elegans development and the timing of N-MYRF release coincides with the onset of synaptic rewiring.
evidence: This is a key finding presented in the abstract.

claim: The timing of N-MYRF release coincides with the onset of synaptic rewiring.
source: We surprisingly find that MYRF trafficking to cell membrane before cleavage is pivotal for C. elegans development and the timing of N-MYRF release coincides with the onset of synaptic rewiring.
evidence: This is a key finding presented in the abstract.

claim: PAN-1 and MYRF interact with each other via their extracellular regions on cell membrane.
source: On cell membrane PAN-1 and MYRF interact with each other via their extracellular regions.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Loss of PAN-1 abolishes MYRF cell membrane localization.
source: Loss of PAN-1 abolishes MYRF cell membrane localization, consequently blocking myrf-dependent neuronal rewiring process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Loss of PAN-1 blocks myrf-dependent neuronal rewiring process.
source: Loss of PAN-1 abolishes MYRF cell membrane localization, consequently blocking myrf-dependent neuronal rewiring process.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: Six GABAergic motor neurons (DD neurons) reverse their axonal and dendritic domains at the end of larval stage 1 (L1) in C. elegans.
source: A striking and informative example of circuit plasticity occurs during the development of the C. elegans nervous system, in which six GABAergic motor neurons, known as dorsal D (DD) neurons, reverse their axonal and dendritic domains at the end of larval stage 1 (L1), with no overt changes in morphology (Hallam and Jin, 1998; White et al., 1978).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to prior work.

claim: DD neurons acquire new connectivity within the motor circuit after completion of synaptic rewiring.
source: After completion of the synaptic rewiring (or remodeling), DD neurons acquire new connectivity within the motor circuit.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Synaptic rewiring of DD neurons is driven by myrf, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian Myrf.
source: Synaptic rewiring of DD neurons is driven by myrf, Caenorhabditis elegans ortholog of mammalian Myrf (Myelin regulatory factor) (Meng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Myrf family consists of conserved, membrane-associated transcription factors.
source: Myrf family consists of conserved, membrane-associated transcription factors.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Germline deletion of Myrf in mice led to early embryonic lethality.
source: In mice, germline deletion of Myrf led to early embryonic lethality (Bujalka et al., 2013), and oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of Myrf blocked myelin formation (Emery et al., 2009; Koenning et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of Myrf in mice blocked myelin formation.
source: In mice, germline deletion of Myrf led to early embryonic lethality (Bujalka et al., 2013), and oligodendrocyte-specific deletion of Myrf blocked myelin formation (Emery et al., 2009; Koenning et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: The null mutation of C. elegans myrf-1 resulted in developmental arrest at the end of L1.
source: The null mutation of C. elegans myrf-1 resulted in developmental arrest at the end of L1, and a partial loss of function mutant of myrf-1 displayed an extra L4-adult molt, indicating that myrf-1 is involved in multi-stage development (Meng et al., 2017; Russel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: More than 30 human genetic variants of MYRF have been identified in patients as causes of developmental anomalies in a range of tissues.
source: Over several years, more than 30 human genetic variants of MYRF have been identified in patients as causes of developmental anomalies in a range of tissues, including heart, lungs, diaphragm, genitourinary tract, and eyes (Qi et al., 2018; Rossetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Human MYRF appeared to be haploinsufficient.
source: In these cases, human MYRF appeared to be haploinsufficient.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from genetic studies.

claim: Mouse Myrf transcriptionally regulates expression of myelinogenesis-related genes in oligodendrocytes.
source: The founding member of the Myrf family, mouse Myrf, transcriptionally regulates expression of myelinogenesis-related genes in oligodendrocytes (Bujalka et al., 2013; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: The transcriptional activity of MYRF is conferred by an N-terminal fragment (N-MYRF) which harbors an Immunoglobulin-fold like DNA-binding domain.
source: The transcriptional activity is conferred by an N-terminal fragment of MYRF (N-MYRF), which harbors an Immunoglobulin (Ig)-fold like DNA-binding domain (DBD) homologous to the DBD of Ndt80, a pleiotropic transcription factor in yeast (Bujalka et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2018; Li et al., 2013; Zhen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Full-length MYRF is localized on ER membrane by its single-pass transmembrane domain in cultured cells.
source: At least in cultured cells, full-length MYRF is localized on ER membrane by its single-pass transmembrane domain and undergoes self-catalyzed proteolysis to release N-MYRF (Bujalka et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: MYRF undergoes self-catalyzed proteolysis to release N-MYRF in cultured cells.
source: At least in cultured cells, full-length MYRF is localized on ER membrane by its single-pass transmembrane domain and undergoes self-catalyzed proteolysis to release N-MYRF (Bujalka et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Cleavage of MYRF is mediated by an intramolecular chaperone of endosialidase (ICE) domain.
source: Cleavage is mediated by an intramolecular chaperone of endosialidase (ICE) domain, located carboxyl to the cleavage point (Schwarzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: MYRF is the only eukaryotic protein known to contain the ICE domain.
source: MYRF is the only eukaryotic protein known to contain the ICE domain, and in MYRF the domain appears to have adopted its ancestral role—to mediate MYRF trimerization and catalyze cleavage (Kim et al., 2017; Li et al., 2013; Meng et al., 2017; Senoo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Cleavage of MYRF on the ER-membrane appears to be constitutive in cultured cells.
source: Cleavage of MYRF on the ER-membrane appears to be constitutive in cultured cells, for which the MYRF ICE domain has been renamed as an intramolecular chaperone auto-cleavage (ICA) domain (Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Over-expression of N-MYRF-1 drives precocious synaptic rewiring in C. elegans.
source: Curiously, while over-expression of N-MYRF-1 drives precocious synaptic rewiring, over-expression of full-length MYRF-1 does not.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Over-expression of full-length MYRF-1 does not drive precocious synaptic rewiring in C. elegans.
source: Curiously, while over-expression of N-MYRF-1 drives precocious synaptic rewiring, over-expression of full-length MYRF-1 does not.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: When MYRF was over-expressed in C. elegans, MYRF protein accumulated in a cytoplasmic structure (likely ER) without increasing in the nucleus.
source: When MYRF was over-expressed in C. elegans, even by modest quantities, MYRF protein accumulated in a cytoplasmic structure (likely ER) without increasing in the nucleus (Meng et al., 2017; Russel et al., 2011), suggesting that MYRF nuclear localization does not automatically occur.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: Ce MYRF is localized to the ER but cannot be cleaved when expressed in human cell lines.
source: In addition, when expressed in human cell lines, Ce MYRF is localized to the ER but cannot be cleaved (Meng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 are together indispensable for driving the synaptic rewiring.
source: Because MYRF-1 and its paralog MYRF-2 are together indispensable for driving the synaptic rewiring (Meng et al., 2017), unraveling the regulation of MYRF activity is key to understanding this plastic process.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work.

claim: PAN-1 was identified as a factor with high binding specificity to both MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 by IP-MS analysis.
source: We identified an LRR-TM protein PAN-1 (M88.6) as a factor with high binding specificity to both MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1A showing IP-MS data.

claim: When PAN-1GFP was pulled down, MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 were found among the most specific interactors of PAN-1.
source: Inversely, when PAN-1GFP (a pan-1GFP knock-in allele) was pulled down using similar procedures, MYRF-1 and MYRF-2 were found among the most specific interactors of PAN-1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: MYRF and PAN-1 can form a protein complex in vivo.
source: The results of the three IP-MS analyses indicate that MYRF and PAN-1 can form a protein complex in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from IP-MS experiments.

claim: MYRF-1 could be co-immunoprecipitated with PAN-1 when both proteins were expressed in HEK293T cells.
source: When both proteins were expressed in HEK293T cells, MYRF-1 could be co-immunoprecipitated with PAN-1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B showing co-IP data.

claim: MYRF and PAN-1 likely interact directly.
source: Because C. elegans proteins were expressed in human cells in this experiment, it is likely that MYRF and PAN-1 interact directly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the co-IP experiment in human cells.

claim: Synaptic remodeling of DD neurons normally occurs at late L1 when new synapses form in the dorsal processes.
source: Synaptic remodeling of DD neurons normally occurs at late L1 when new synapses form in the dorsal processes of DD neurons, which is marked by the dorsal appearance of clusters of synaptic vesicles (Figure 1C–E; Hallam and Jin, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation and supported by Figure 1C-E.

claim: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants.
source: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants (Figure 1D,E), indicating that the synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D,E showing synaptic marker images.

claim: Synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
source: By late L1, few synapses had formed in the dorsal processes of DDs in pan-1(gk142) mutants (Figure 1D,E), indicating that the synaptic remodeling was defective in pan-1 mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D,E.

claim: Axon morphology of DDs in pan-1(gk142) was no different from control animals.
source: Axon morphology of DDs in pan-1(gk142) was no different from control animals; if anything, the GFP intensity of dorsal processes in pan-1(gk142) appeared to be weaker (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1F.

claim: The defective synaptic rewiring in pan-1(gk142) had not improved by the end of L2 (28 post-hatch hours).
source: The defective synpatic rewiring had not improved by the end of L2 (28 post-hatch hours) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of pan-1 does not generally affect synaptogenesis in DDs.
source: The presence of juvenile DD synapses in pan-1 mutants suggests that the loss of pan-1 does not generally affect synaptogenesis in DDs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the observation of ventral synapses.

claim: pan-1 is expressed broadly in embryos and larvae.
source: pan-1 is expressed broadly in embryos and larvae (Gao et al., 2012; Gissendanner and Kelley, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citation to prior work.

claim: Expression of pan-1b driven by unc-25pro restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants.
source: Expression of longest isoform pan-1b driven by unc-25pro (expressed in DD and VD) restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants, while the other two isoforms, pan-1a or pan-1c could not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: pan-1a and pan-1c isoforms could not restore the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants.
source: Expression of longest isoform pan-1b driven by unc-25pro (expressed in DD and VD) restored the synaptic remodeling defects in pan-1 mutants, while the other two isoforms, pan-1a or pan-1c could not (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Expression of pan-1 driven by flp-13pro rescued synaptic rewiring defects in pan-1 mutants.
source: Furthermore, expression of pan-1 (referring to pan-1b hereafter) driven by flp-13pro (expressed in DD not VD among ventral cord motor neurons) also rescued synaptic rewiring defects in pan-1 mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Specific expression of pan-1 in muscles, epidermis, or intestine did not mitigate the deficient synaptic remodeling in pan-1(0).
source: In contrast, specific expression of pan-1 in muscles, epidermis, or intestine did not mitigate the deficient synaptic remodeling in pan-1(0) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PAN-1B regulates synaptic remodeling in DDs cell autonomously.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that a transmembrane isoform of PAN-1, PAN-1B, regulates synaptic remodeling in DDs cell autonomously; in other words, restoring PAN-1 in DDs is sufficient to promote synaptic rewiring in developmentally arrested mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from rescue experiments.

claim: PAN-1GFP signal was detected broadly in embryos and early larvae, but decreased substantially in late larvae and adults.
source: PAN-1GFP signal was detected broadly in embryos and early larvae, but decreased substantially in late larvae and adults (Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two types of PAN-1GFP subcellular patterns were observed: at the cell membrane and as cytoplasmic puncta.
source: Two types of PAN-1GFP subcellular patterns were observed: at the cell membrane and as cytoplasmic puncta.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: PAN-1 distributed at the lateral basal membrane of seam cells.
source: By colabelling a tight-junction component DLG-1::RFP and PAN-1GFP (Figure 3B), we observed that PAN-1 distributed at the lateral basal membrane of seam cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing colocalization.

claim: PAN-1 is localized on the cell membrane of many ventral cord neurons, including DD neurons at L1 and L2.
source: PAN-1 is also localized on the cell membrane of many ventral cord neurons, including DD neurons at L1 and L2 (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3C,D.

claim: Deleting either the SP or TMD of PAN-1 caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity.
source: Deleting either the SP or TMD caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity, suggesting that PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
source: Deleting either the SP or TMD caused PAN-1 to lose its rescuing activity, suggesting that PAN-1's membrane localization is required for its function.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from deletion experiments.

claim: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function.
source: We found that the cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function; in contrast, the LRR domains, the main motifs within the extracellular region, were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The LRR domains of PAN-1 were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
source: We found that the cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was not essential for its function; in contrast, the LRR domains, the main motifs within the extracellular region, were necessary for PAN-1's activity in synaptic remodeling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: In early L1 larvae, MYRF-1GFP signal was observed at the cell membrane of many cell types, but were not obviously enriched in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
source: In early L1 larvae, GFP signal was observed at the cell membrane of many cell types, including pharynx, epidermis, and neurons, but were not obviously enriched in the cytoplasm or nucleus (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B,C.

claim: Toward late L1 stage, MYRF-1GFP signals started to appear in the nucleus.
source: Toward late L1 stage, GFP signals started to appear in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Within a stage-synchronized population, animals exhibited variable patterns of MYRF-1GFP's localization.
source: Within a stage-synchronized population, animals exhibited variable patterns of MYRF-1GFP's localization, that is primarily at the cell membrane, primarily in the nucleus, or both at the cell membrane and in the nucleus (Figure 4B–F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4B–F.

claim: Cell-membrane-to-nucleus transition of MYRF-1GFP was observed in DD neurons.
source: By colabeling with DD-expressing mCherry::Rab-3, we observed cell-membrane-to-nucleus transition of MYRF-1GFP in DD neurons (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E,F.

claim: MYRF-2GFP exhibited stronger signals than MYRF-1GFP in early L1 larvae.
source: A similar early-stage cell membrane-localization was observed for MYRF-2GFP, the paralog of MYRF-1, except that MYRF-2GFP exhibited stronger signals than MYRF-1GFP in early L1 larvae (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: MYRF-2GFP displayed the trend of localization transitioning from cell membrane to nucleus during L1 development.
source: MYRF-2GFP also displayed the trend of localization transitioning from cell membrane to nucleus during L1 development.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: MYRFGFP is localized primarily at cell membrane in early L1 animals, and becomes increasingly localized in the nucleus as larval development progresses.
source: Together, we observed that MYRFGFP is localized primarily at cell membrane in early L1 animals, and becomes increasingly localized in the nucleus as larval development progresses.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of observations.

claim: myrf-1S483A K488A GFP allele caused a larval arrest in animals, similar to the arrest observed in myrf-1 null mutants.
source: This myrf-1S483A K488A GFP allele caused a larval arrest in animals (Figure 5B,C), similar to the arrest observed in myrf-1 null mutants and consistent with our previous finding that myrf-1's activity is cleavage-dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B,C.

claim: MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was only detected at the cell membrane but not in the nucleus at any viable stages.
source: Importantly, MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was only detected at the cell membrane but not in the nucleus at any viable stages (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5D–G.

claim: The intensity of MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was increased compared to wild type.
source: The intensity of MYRF-1S483A K488A GFP was increased compared to wild type, in accordance with our prediction that mutant MYRF would accumulate on cell membrane because it cannot be cleaved.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The overall course of synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP was similar to myrf-1(ybq6), a putative null indel allele.
source: The overall course of synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP was similar to myrf-1(ybq6), a putative null indel allele, although the synaptic rewiring in myrf-1S483A K488A GFP appeared to be less complete than myrf-1(ybq6) (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: When myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated with myrf-1S483A K488A GFP, the synaptic rewiring was severely blocked.
source: When myrf-2, the paralog of myrf-1, was simultaneously mutated, the synaptic rewiring was severely blocked (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 7–12), consistent with our previous finding that myrf-1 and myrf-2 are together indispensable for synaptic rewiring in DDs.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: MYRF is associated with cell membrane before cleavage, which is temporally controlled during development.
source: These data support that MYRF is associated with cell membrane before cleavage, which is temporally controlled during development.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the loss-of-cleavage mutant analysis.

claim: PAN-1 binding was observed with the C-terminal region of MYRF, but not with the N-terminal region.
source: PAN-1 binding was observed with the C-terminal region of MYRF, but not with the N-terminal region (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7B showing co-IP results.

claim: PAN-1 may use its non-cytoplasmic LRR domains to interact with the non-cytoplasmic region of MYRF.
source: This result is consistent with their topographic configuration on ER membrane, which predicts that PAN-1 may use its non-cytoplasmic LRR domains to interact with the non-cytoplasmic region of MYRF.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the co-IP results.

claim: The LRR domains of PAN-1 was responsible for binding with C-MYRF.
source: The LRR domains of PAN-1 was responsible for binding with C-MYRF (Figure 7C); the binding occurred when the two fragments coexisted either in the ER lumen or cytoplasm of HEK cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7C.

claim: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was dispensable for PAN-1's binding with MYRF.
source: The cytoplasmic region of PAN-1 was dispensable for PAN-1's binding with MYRF.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: PAN-1 uses its LRR domain to interact with the extracellular region of MYRF.
source: Together these data indicate that PAN-1 uses its LRR domain to interact with the extracellular region of MYRF.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from deletion experiments.

claim: myrf-11-700 GFP deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2.
source: This deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2, indicating that the extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claim: The extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function.
source: This deletion allele was recessive and homozygous mutants exhibited larval arrest at L2, indicating that the extracellular domain of MYRF-1 was necessary for normal function (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages.
source: Importantly, MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), showing that the extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D–F and supplement.

claim: The extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
source: Importantly, MYRF-11-700 GFP displayed prominent cytoplasmic signals while its cell-membrane or nuclear localization were not obvious at any viable stages (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), showing that the extracellular domain is required for MYRF's proper localization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8D–F and supplement.

claim: myrf-11-790 GFP mutant displayed larval arrest at L2.
source: myrf-11-790 GFP mutant also displayed larval arrest at L2 (Figure 8B,C) and prominent cytoplasmic GFP signal instead of cell membrane or nuclear signals (Figure 8D–F; Figure 8—figure supplement 1), supporting that that the extracellular region of MYRF is functionally critical.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8B,C.

claim: The extracellular region of MYRF-2 was necessary for MYRF-2's cell membrane localization.
source: Using a similar strategy, we analyzed an in-frame deletion allele myrf-21-728 GFP and found that the extracellular region of MYRF-2 was necessary for MYRF-2's cell membrane localization because MYRF-21-728 was primarily detected in cytoplasm (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: myrf-11-790 GFP allele exhibited blocked synaptic rewiring under myrf-2 null background.
source: myrf-11-790 GFP allele, in which a part of the extracellular domain of MYRF was removed, exhibited blocked synaptic rewiring under myrf-2 null background (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–12), a phenotype similarly observed in myrf-1(ybq6).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: myrf-11-700 GFP allele exhibited precocious synaptic rewiring.
source: In contrast, myrf-11-700 GFP allele, in which the whole extracellular region of MYRF is lost, exhibited precocious synaptic rewiring, that is clearly detectable synaptic puncta formed in the dorsal processes of DDs at 12, 14 post-hatch hours, time points by which synaptic rewiring has not occurred yet in wild type animals (Figure 6; Figure 6—figure supplements 1–12).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: The precocious synaptic rewiring in myrf-11-700 GFP allele also occurred in myrf-2(0) background.
source: The precocious synaptic rewiring in myrf-11-700 GFP allele also occurred in myrf-2(0) background.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The precocious dorsal synapses in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants were not uniformly distributed along the dorsal cord.
source: Notably, the precocious dorsal synapses in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants were not uniformly distributed along the dorsal cord, that is in some DDs the remodeling occurred while in the rest the remodeling did not, even though they were in the same animal, implying that the observed precocity in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants was not a strictly regulated event.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: myrf-11-700 GFP caused an advancement in M-cell lineage progression at 12, 14, and 16 post-hatch hours.
source: We found that myrf-11-700 GFP caused an advancement in M-cell lineage progression at 12, 14, and 16 post-hatch hours (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9A.

claim: This advancement in M-cell lineage was eliminated when myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated.
source: Curiously, this advancement was eliminated when myrf-2 was simultaneously mutated (as a putative indel null); even more so, M-cell division was delayed in myrf-11-700 GFP; myrf-2(0) double mutants (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9A.

claim: The synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell).
source: By dual-labeling M-cell progenitors and synapses of DDs in the same individuals, we determined that the synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell); this coordination of timing was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants because many animals had displayed rewired dorsal synapses while only containing less than 4 M-cell progeny cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B.

claim: The coordination of timing between synaptic rewiring and M-cell division was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants.
source: By dual-labeling M-cell progenitors and synapses of DDs in the same individuals, we determined that the synaptic rewiring was normally initiated when the M-cell underwent the 4th M-cell division (8 + cell); this coordination of timing was disrupted in myrf-11-700 GFP mutants because many animals had displayed rewired dorsal synapses while only containing less than 4 M-cell progeny cells (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B.

claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were consistently brighter than MYRF-11-790 GFP signals.
source: The first was that MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were consistently brighter than MYRF-11-790 GFP signals although they were both predominantly cytoplasmic (Figure 8G; Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 8G and supplement.

claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were observed in nuclei of many cells.
source: A more striking feature was that the MYRF-11-700 GFP signals were observed in nuclei of many cells, which is especially evident in big nuclei such as those for seam cells, epidermal cells, and intestinal cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: Similar nuclear GFP signals were not observed in myrf-11-790 GFP mutants.
source: In contrast, similar nuclear GFP signals were not observed in myrf-11-790 GFP mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: The distribution of PAN-1GFP in myrf-1(ju1121) mutants was comparable to that in wild type animals.

claim: myrf-1 is unlikely to regulate PAN-1's stability or trafficking.

claim: MYRF-1GFP or MYRF-2GFP signal, both on the membrane and in the nucleus, was barely detected in pan-1 mutants at all stages examined.

claim: PAN-1 critically regulates MYRF localization.
source: In stark contrast, MYRF-1GFP or MYRF-2GFP signal, both on the membrane and in the nucleus, was barely detected in pan-1 mutants at all stages examined (Figure 10A; Figure 10—figure supplement 1A), indicating that PAN-1 critically regulates MYRF localization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10A and supplement.

claim: The loss of MYRFGFP in pan-1(0) was not due to failed transcription of myrf genes.
source: The loss of MYRFGFP in pan-1(0) was not due to failed transcription of myrf genes, as myrf-1 and myrf-2 transcript levels were not significantly changed in pan-1(0) mutants (Figure 10B).

claim: MYRF proteins are subject to proteasome degradation in the absence of PAN-1.
source: When critical regulators of the proteasome system were knocked down in pan-1(0) animals, MYRFGFP signals re-emerged in many cells, indicating that MYRF proteins are subject to proteasome degradation in the absence of PAN-1.

claim: Restored MYRFGFP in pan-1 mutants was not localized to the cell membrane or nucleus; rather, the signal appeared in ER-like structures in the cytoplasm.
source: Importantly, restored MYRFGFP in pan-1 mutants was not localized to the cell membrane or nucleus; rather, the signal appeared in ER-like structures in the cytoplasm, suggesting that interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF initiates when they are in ER.

claim: Interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF initiates when they are in ER.

claim: PAN-1 is necessary for normal localization and function of MYRF.
source: In conclusion, PAN-1 is necessary for normal localization and function of MYRF.

claim: Exogenously expressed pan-1 can restore the cell-membrane localization of MYRF in pan-1 mutants.
source: We used a seam cell-specific promoter to drive pan-1 expression (Figure 10D) and observed restored nuclear MYRF-1GFP signal in seam cells of pan-1(0) animals, indicating that MYRF had been normally localized and processed in those cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10D.

claim: MYRF-11-700 GFP signals remained strong in pan-1(0) mutants.

claim: PAN-1 is essential for stabilizing MYRF and trafficking it to cell membrane.
source: Therefore, PAN-1 is essential for stabilizing MYRF and trafficking it to cell membrane.

claim: Overexpression of the extracellular region of MYRF-1 in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling.
source: Overexpression of either fusion protein (TMD::MYRF-1681-931 and SP:: MYRF-1681-931) in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling, supporting that the interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.

claim: The interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.
source: Overexpression of either fusion protein (TMD::MYRF-1681-931 and SP:: MYRF-1681-931) in DD neurons blocked synaptic remodeling, supporting that the interaction between PAN-1 and MYRF is important for MYRF activity.

claim: ER-retained PAN-1 impeded the rewiring processes drastically.
source: The ER-retained PAN-1 indeed impeded the rewiring processes drastically, as the dorsal synapses were greatly reduced and most of the juvenile ventral synapses were sustained by 28 post-hatch hours.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: When ER-retained PAN-1 was expressed in DDs and seam cells, MYRFGFP signals were primarily cytoplasmic showing a pattern similar to ER structures.
source: When ER-retained PAN-1 was expressed in DDs as well as seam cells of animals carrying myrf-1GFP, we observed much brighter MYRFGFP signals in target cells than in neighbor cells, and importantly, the signals were primarily cytoplasmic showing a pattern similar to ER structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section.

claim: PAN-1 promotes MYRF's transport to cell membrane.

claim: PAN-1 interacting with MYRF in ER is insufficient for MYRF's cleavage.
